title: The scientist sent to change RFK Jr’s mind on vaccines
transcript:
Speaker 1: My mother, when she found out you were coming on, she's a big Democrat, she says, he's dangerous. He's an anti-vaxxer. He says that autism comes from vaccines and you must challenge him on that, Jesse.
Speaker 2: Is my mom crazy?
Speaker 3: Well, I do believe that autism does come from vaccines.
Speaker 2: Robert F.
Speaker 4: Kennedy Jr. has spent years making false claims about vaccines.
Speaker 3: There's no vaccine that is, you know, safe and effective.
Speaker 4: Today, he's in charge of America's health department.
Speaker 2: Will you reassure mothers, unequivocally and without qualification, that the measles and hepatitis B vaccines do not cause autism?
Speaker 3: Senator, I am not going into the agency with any.
Speaker 2: That's kind of a yes or no question.
Speaker 4: Nearly a decade ago, the US government's top expert in infectious diseases, Anthony Fauci, asked vaccine scientist Peter Hotez to speak to RFK Jr. to try and convince him that vaccines don't cause autism. he couldn't change his mind. Now, Hotez is watching those same ideas become part of a much bigger movement, fuelled by political power, money and an industry profiting off the distrust of medicine. I'm Ruby Jones, and you're listening to 7am. Today, Professor Peter Hotez on his history with Robert F.
Speaker 2: Kennedy Jr.
Speaker 4: the rise of America's anti-vaccine movement, and why he's warning Australia to pay attention. It's Monday, November 23. Peter, hello and welcome to 7am. It's great to have you on the show.
Speaker 2: Great to be on. Thanks so much.
Speaker 4: So Peter, I thought we could begin, if you don't mind, by going back to 2017. You were asked by Anthony Fauci to have this chat.
Speaker 5: With Robert F.
Speaker 2: Kennedy Jr.
Speaker 4: And try to convince him that vaccines don't cause autism. Can you tell me a bit about that conversation?
Speaker 2: Yeah, it was in my office and my assistant said, hey, Dr. Hotez, I got these two gentlemen on the phone and she's reading the names. One's Dr. Anthony Fauci and the other one's Dr. Francis Collins, who's, of course, the director of the National Institutes of Health. And they were having discussions with Mr. Kennedy and thought that given my experiences, not only as a vaccine scientist and a pediatrician, but also having a daughter, Rachel, our youngest daughter has autism and intellectual disabilities. Now she's an adult. And I'd been explaining to audiences off and on why vaccines don't cause autism based on both the science and my personal experiences. They thought that Bobby should at least hear me out. And as you can see, I was not very effective. And, uh, It didn't go terribly well, but it was at least every time he said something that was misinformed, I would actually go to the biomedical literature, the PubMed database, which is the major database from the U.S. National Library of Medicine that doctors all over the world use to refute all of his statements. And before I know it, I had a pretty good pile of notes. So afterwards, I decided to turn it into a book. And that wound up making me public enemy number one or two with anti-vaccine groups. But it also gave me a front row seat to understanding what this is all about and watched how this anti-science movement has shifted or morphed over the last three decades.
Speaker 4: And as you say, I mean, your work has really put you in the public eye and also in the firing line somewhat. In 2023, there was that moment where Joe Rogan challenged you to debate the RFK Jr.
Speaker 2: On his podcast.
Speaker 5: Rogan responded in kind Saturday, challenging Hotez to debate RFK Jr., tweeting, quote, Peter, if you claim what RFK Jr. is saying is misinformation, I am offering you $ 100, 000 to the charity of your choice if you're willing to debate him on my show with.
Speaker 2: No time limit.
Speaker 4: Elon Musk then, he kind of joined in those calls for you to take part. You refused to go on, but things got pretty nasty around that time. Tell me a bit about what happened.
Speaker 2: Yeah, by then I had every follower on Twitter against me, except for the ones following Taylor Swift. It was quite extraordinary just watching this thing unfold. So Mr. Kennedy had gone on the Joe Rogan podcast, and I had gone on earlier before Joe kind of went down that anti-vaccine rabbit hole. And And it was mostly fine.
Speaker 6: Thanks for being here. I appreciate it. It's good to see you again.
Speaker 2: Well, thank you for raising awareness of all this stuff. I really appreciate it, Joe.
Speaker 3: My pleasure.
Speaker 6: My pleasure. And I appreciate you coming down here and explaining a lot of this stuff for us.
Speaker 2: It's been a great time. But, you know, he decided to taunt me into debating Mr. Kennedy when he was running for president. And... You know, having a full year of discussions with RFK Jr. back in 2017, I knew they would not be productive because I learned about him that he's not interested in the science or can't understand the science. And so there'd be no scientific rationale for having those discussions. And I realized what they really wanted from me was to create an exhibition or a show. And by pairing Mr. Kennedy with a serious scientist, it was a way to legitimize his run for presidency, and I didn't want to help him. But I think most importantly, I didn't want to send the message to young people that this is how we do science. Sure, you had, in the 1920s, you had Albert Einstein and Niels Bohr having public discussions about quantum physics, but But that's very different. Those are two colleagues who respected each other and were really trying to figure something out with their peers. This was nothing like this. This was going to be the Jerry Springer show. And that's not what I wanted to do.
Speaker 4: And those private conversations with RFK Jr., were there things that you felt like you could influence him on? Was there any kind of common.
Speaker 2: Ground at all? You know, back then, this is when the publications were coming out. the first group of autism genes, and they're all involved in early fetal brain development. And that's the basis of autism. It has a very strong genetic basis. And we even wound up doing genomic sequencing on my daughter, Rachel, and my wife, Ann, and I, and we found Rachel's autism gene. But it doesn't mean that there's no environmental interactions. So in my conversations with Mr. Kennedy, I'd say, Bobby, you know, there's two or three known environmental exposures all early on in pregnancy that can influence autism genes. And I said, look, you're an environmental attorney. This is your moment. This is your sweet spot. This is what you should be focusing on. And you could actually make a positive difference in the world if you can expand that list and really understand all of the environmental exposures interacting with autism genes. That would be a real public service. And And it was quite frustrating for me. I couldn't engage him on it. He just didn't want to listen. He had no interest in understanding about autism genes. He had no interest in the known chemical exposures linked to autism and kept on pushing the false narrative around vaccines. And it was frustrating for me that he and his colleagues to this day still have no interest in really understanding that.
Speaker 4: Coming up, Who's profiting from America's anti-vaccine movement?
Speaker 3: The CDC recommended a COVID vaccine without any scientific basis. or six-year-old children. Most experts agree today, even the people who did it back then, that COVID vaccines are inappropriate for six-year-old children who basically have a zero risk from COVID.
Speaker 4: Let's talk a bit more about the anti-vaccine movement, because obviously it's grown a lot since you first spoke with RFK Jr. What impact do you think his position as health secretary, this platform that he's been given, has had on the movement?
Speaker 2: Well, the movement had gained already a lot of steam even before Mr. Kennedy became Health and Human Services Secretary. We really saw it come off the rails during the COVID pandemic. I mean, it had been, you know, if you want to take a step back and look at the timeline, you know, you have the original claims, false claims that vaccines cause autism going back to 1998. And then about 12 years ago, 13 years ago, this is when the movement took kind of a political turn under this banner of health freedom, medical freedom. You know, you can't tell us what to do. And this is when anti-vaccine groups started getting what's called PAC money, political action committee money, to pay for candidates to run on anti-vaccine platforms to introduce anti-vaccine legislation. And that's what really came off the rails during COVID-19. You saw this under this rubric of health freedom, medical freedom. You started to see initially this big pushback against COVID vaccine mandates. It was followed by a parade of anti-vaccine advocates. activists and talking heads on television falsely discrediting the effectiveness, the safety of COVID vaccines. So it started out. With a representative from North Carolina would use rhetoric like first they're going to vaccinate you, then they're going to take away your guns and your Bibles. Mask mandates are dying because patriots have fought back.
Speaker 6: Let's do it again with vaccine mandates.
Speaker 2: This is not a matter of health. It's a matter of liberty. And then Fox News did the same thing, and Fox News did a lot of damage.
Speaker 1: We are going to give it everything we have to make sure that students are not going to have to live in a medical apartheid because they don't want to get the vaccine.
Speaker 2: Bringing on all the talking heads to falsely discredit the effectiveness and safety of vaccines. So maybe it doesn't work, and they're simply not telling you that. Well, you hate to think that, especially if you've gotten two shots. And then Joe Rogan did the same thing.
Speaker 6: If you're like 21 years old and you say to me, should I get vaccinated? I go, no. Are you healthy? Are you a healthy person? Like, look, don't do anything stupid, but you should take care of yourself.
Speaker 2: My estimate is at least 200,000 Americans needlessly perished because they refused a COVID vaccine. And this is why I became so.
Speaker 2: Worked so hard to debunk it because now it's a lethal force in America.
Speaker 5: A new COVID-19 variant is now spreading across the United States.
Speaker 2: A new COVID variant is showing up in more than two dozen states.
Speaker 3: New CDC data shows cases are rising in more than half the country.
Speaker 2: I felt uniquely positioned given the fact that I was going on the cable news channels regularly because we had, because I had, among the vaccines that our group had made was coronavirus vaccines for the original SARS and MERS, the first two major COVID epidemics. And then SARS-2, which is the cause of COVID-19, we pivoted and made a low-cost COVID vaccine that reached 100 million people in India and Indonesia with no patents. And so did as best I could, but the problem was I was cut off from reaching the people that I needed the most. And because I was going on Fox News early on in the pandemic. And then when I refused to go along with the hydroxychloroquine nonsense, they stopped inviting me.
Speaker 4: And you mentioned the enormous amounts of money flowing through political action committees to back candidates who support an anti-science agenda. So tell me a bit about who is behind that money and what they stand to gain.
Speaker 2: So that's something that still largely remains uninvestigated. Clearly, now the wellness and influencer industry is putting a lot of money into this because they profit from pushing alternatives. And if you ever wondered why there are always small molecule antiparasitic drugs like ivermectin or hydroxychloroquine or fenbendazole. It's because you can buy them up in bulk for very low cost. You can then repackage them, put your own label on it, jack up the price a hundredfold, and oftentimes sell it with a very expensive, maybe $ 1, 000 telehealth visit. It's a very corrupt industry. But for that to work, you have to denigrate mainstream science. And it's interesting how Mr. Kennedy has changed his rhetoric from when I spoke to him 10 years ago, Some of his talking points are the same, you know, that claiming that MMR vaccine causes autism, or he says the MMR vaccine is contaminated with aborted fetal remnants and this kind of nonsense. That's the old Mr. Kennedy. The new version says, well, you could also get an infusion of vitamin A, budesonide, and clarithromycin, and you're scratching your head saying, where did that come from? And then you realize this is all the wellness influencer stuff. industry. So it's really a whole anti-science ecosystem that's both politically motivated and financially motivated as well.
Speaker 4: And you're in Australia this week, and you've warned that the same anti-vaccine movement can easily spread here. We've already seen childhood vaccination rates decline in Australia. So what lessons do you think that we should be taking from the way this has played out in the U.S.
Speaker 2: Well, first of all, I'm here for also scientific reasons because I have longstanding scientific collaborations with Australian scientists. One of the things that I would often say when I would do ABC interviews during the pandemic is the Australian science punches above its weight in the areas of infection and immunology. But I think the other is to at least describe what the anti-vaccine ecosystem looks like in the United States to avoid potentially the same kind of politically motivated attacks on science or financially motivated attacks on science from happening elsewhere. Because I think too often we're starting to see the spread of U.S.-style anti-vaccine activism into other countries. We're seeing it in parts of Canada, for instance, particularly in southern Alberta. You're seeing it In parts of Mexico, you're seeing it linked with the AFD party in Germany. And so far, Australia, I think, has been pretty good at holding the line. But I think it's useful to educate people what this is all about so you can head it off at the pass before it starts to grow and gain momentum.
Speaker 4: Well, Professor, thank you so much for your time today.
Speaker 2: Well, thank you so much.
Speaker 6: Also in the news, former New South Wales MP and figurehead of the right-wing Christian Democratic Party, Reverend Fred Nile, has died aged 92. A controversial figure, Nile was best known for his staunch opposition to same-sex marriage and abortion.
Speaker 4: But in his later years, the Christian Conservatives supported legislation expunging homosexual convictions and also teamed up with Gay MP Alex Greenidge on legislation protecting Indigenous culture and heritage.
Speaker 6: And Defence Minister Richard Marles has rebuffed a report from the US Congressional Budget Office which found the Yorker Submarine Agreement would put a strain on the already struggling US Navy.
Speaker 2: Miles says the report is wrong and that production is improving. I'm Daniel James. Thanks for listening to 7am. We'll be back tomorrow.
